events.text:
🇹🇷 Turkey’s quiet Black Sea shipping squeeze – what if it becomes permanent?
 
🔴 The Turkish authority responsible for the monitoring and management of heavy commercial cargoes through the Bosporus and the Dardanelles has reportedly started restricting the passage of vessels bound to and from Russian and Ukrainian ports.
🔴 Sources told Bloomberg the Directorate General of Coastal Safety has implemented de facto restrictions by halting the issuance of transit permits, or deliberately dragging out the review of applications. Ships bound for Turkish, Bulgarian, Romanian and Georgian ports are being allowed to proceed as normal.
🔴 The restrictions come in the wake of a series of drone attacks on Turkish-flagged and owned vessels, plus the targeting of Russian compressor stations linked to TurkStream and Blue Stream gas pipeline infrastructure. Up to 10 crew members have been killed and 7 injured in the last month.
 
Implications
 
➡️ the restrictions stretch the limits of Turkey’s legal authority under the 1936 Montreux Convention, which guarantees “absolute freedom of navigation” for commercial vessels. If they become permanent, that opens the door for other countries in command of natural or manmade maritime passages doing the same (Egypt, Panama, Spain, Iran, Yemen, Indonesia-Malaysia-Singapore, Chile, South Africa, Russia)
➡️ while the restrictions could hurt Russian energy and food exporters, they may absolutely cripple Ukraine, which has no alternative major maritime export routes
➡️ Kazak crude exports (80% of which pass through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal at Novorossiysk) may also be severely affected. There are no viable, large-scale alternatives
➡️ a block on Russian energy exports will exacerbate the global energy crisis caused by the Iran war – pummeling net importers, especially if shipping restrictions are complemented by a shutdown of Turkey-bound natural gas exports, which besides Turkey also feed much of southeastern Europe
➡️ the Black Sea region accounts for up to 20% of global grain exports, 60% of sunflower oil exports, and 15% or more of global mineral fertilizer exports. Unless costly alternative overland routes are found, entire regions and subcontinents, from North Africa to the Middle East, could plunge into economic and political crises

🤥🇮🇷 Trump’s Iran brinksmanship painting him into a corner – and the US out of the Gulf
 
Trump may have believed his own hype, betting that restarting the Iran war would finally deliver the quick victory that eluded him the first time. Instead, Tehran now threatens to hand to hand Washington a defeat even more humiliating than the one delineated in the June 17 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
While the MoU did not include explicit clauses that would strip the US military of its right to navigate Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Iranian officials’ latest terms in talks with Oman include demands that US Navy warships stay out of the area completely.
💬 “The fundamental result is going to be significant Iranian de facto control over the Strait,” former US intel officer Jonathan Panikoff told WSJ.
US officials insist Washington will not accept any deal which allows Iran to collect tolls, or deny access to the Strait.
But given the vast arsenal the IRGC has its disposal to target violating vessels, Washington doesn’t seem to have much leverage in the matter. American warship and carrier strikes groups have already kept well away from the Iranian coastline throughout t the war, fearing ballistic, cruise missile and drone strikes.
Gulf officials have reportedly “acknowledged” that de facto Iranian control over the Strait may be the new normal, and the “best option,” given the impact of its continued closure on global energy markets and regional economies.
 
🤔 History in the making?
 
A US retreat from the Gulf would set back US policy in the region 55 years – back to the 1971 basing agreement with Bahrain, and subsequent[ expansions to bases across Arab Gulf countries.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73010) Iran’s counterstrikes since February showed that these bases are not only defenseless, but pointless when it comes to the protection of America’s Gulf allies. On the contrary – the more US bases a country hosts, the more vulnerable it is to Iranian strikes.
President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated Friday that Iran would do everything in its power to prevent the US and Israel from uniting the Gulf countries against it – starting with the reminder that unlike Israel, Iran has “no intention of attacking other countries, seizing territory or expanding our borders.”

🇮🇱🔍 Why Israeli politicians are desperate to shut Palestinians out of power
Israel's opposition once argued that cooperation with Palestinian Arab parties was key to ending Benjamin Netanyahu's long dominance of Israeli politics.
Now, the same politicians are trying to freeze Palestinian Arabs out of the government, despite the fact that they represent one-fifth of the population.
The pledge has been repeated in recent weeks by figures across the anti-Netanyahu camp, such as Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who used to defend their partnership with Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas as the necessary price of ending Netanyahu’s dominance.
The same stance is shared by Gadi Eisenkot, who has been positioning himself as a potential PM. Opinion polls suggest that at the October election Eisenkot's bloc will be running neck-and-neck with Netanyahu's coalition.
👉 This marks a sharp retreat from the pragmatic experiment of 2021 and shows how the events of October 2023 rewired the political climate around cooperation with Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The latter make up roughly two million people and are descendants of those who remained after the 1948 war.
Their parties have sat on the political margins for decades, and the taboo was broken only in 2021, when Ra’am’s four seats allowed Bennett and Lapid to assemble a majority.
However, that arrangement lasted barely a year. Now, the taboo appears to have returned.
🔴 71.5% of Jewish Israelis oppose including Arab parties in the next government (Israel Democracy Institute)
🔴 57% of Israelis oppose a Palestinian state under any circumstances (Institute for National Security Studies survey)
Political arithmetic may ultimately prove more stubborn than campaign rhetoric since Israel's fragmented parliament has repeatedly produced deadlocks.
Recent polling suggests neither bloc can count on securing a majority alone.
There is also another lingering question: whether the political cost of ignoring Palestinian citizens of Israel will eventually become too high for the Zionist state.
